verses.note: The first fear in Scripture is the terror of a guilty conscience, which drives the sinner away from God. The Bible later speaks of a different fear of the LORD, reverent trust that draws near, and the New Testament speaks of love that casts out fear (1 John 4:18).
Pagan courtiers respond to God's warning with the fear Abraham denied them. Scripture often shows outsiders fearing God more readily than his own people, as with the sailors in Jonah 1:16.

The verse assumes that a people without the fear of God is capable of anything, and in that Abraham is right. His mistake is to assume he can tell who fears God by their nationality. Fear of man drove him to lie, the snare Proverbs 29:25 warns of.
The fear of God is defined here by what a person will not withhold from him. It is reverence shown in action, the same quality for which Job is described as one who feared God (Job 1:1).

The encounter produces fear before it produces worship. Jacob's fear is not terror of punishment but the awe of a man who suddenly knows himself in God's presence, the beginning of wisdom in Proverbs 9:10.

In Genesis the fear of God is what restrains the powerful from abusing the stranger. Abraham feared there was no fear of God in Gerar (20:11), and the Hebrew midwives will spare Israel's sons because they fear God (Exodus 1:17). Joseph holds absolute power over these men, and the fear of God sets the limit on how he uses it.

"Do not be afraid" is God's word to each patriarch in turn (15:1 to Abram, 26:24 to Isaac, here to Jacob). The command rests entirely on who is speaking and what he promises, not on any change in Jacob's circumstances.
The verse defines the fear of God by what it does: it refuses to take innocent life at a king's command. Fear of God here is not terror but a reverence that removes the fear of man.

Moses' fear is not the terror of a guilty man before a tyrant but the awe of a creature before the holy God. The same Moses will later ask to see God's glory (33:18), and God will shelter him while he passes by.

The fear of God that Scripture commends is not terror that flees but reverence that stays and obeys. This verse is one of the clearest statements of the difference: the fear that Moses forbids and the fear he commends are named side by side.

The people's fear at Moses' face is a reflected form of their fear of God. The veil lets them live near the mediator without being overwhelmed, while the unveiled speaking keeps God's word before them.
Fear of the LORD here is not terror but reverent loyalty, and it is the goal of the teaching. Keeping the statutes is the way that reverence shows itself over a lifetime.
Fear and joy are not opposites here. The fear of the LORD is the trembling of those who have seen his majesty, and the joy is that such a king is good.
Praise and awe belong together. Those who fear the LORD are invited to rejoice in what he has done for one of them.
The whole section assumes that God's regard matters more than anyone else's. Living before the Father who sees in secret frees disciples from managing their image.

The women's trembling is the awe of creatures before God's direct act, the same response that met Jesus' stilling of the storm (4:41) and the transfiguration (9:6). Mark does not treat their fear as simple unbelief; he treats it as what happens to human beings when God does what only God can do.
The fear here is awe before God's evident presence. It is the fitting response to the holy, the same response the crowds had to Jesus' miracles (Luke 5:26).

The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7, 9:10), and its absence is the end of Paul's diagnosis. Everything wrong in speech and action flows from a life lived as if God were not watching.
Fear and trembling are the posture of those who know God is at work among them. It is the reverent seriousness of worship, not the terror of the unforgiven.
Fear here is not dread of God's character but seriousness about his promise. The author calls for a holy fear of missing what God offers, the opposite of complacency.
